groups.text: Every change to an order's status must be logged.
You want that logging written once, in a small helper class.
By hand, the property forwards its getter and setter to that helper.
::status is a reference to the property itself, a KProperty.
It knows its name, so the helper can log status without a string.
That forwarding is all by does.
Write by, and the compiler writes the getter and the setter for you.
The helper is called the delegate.
It needs two functions with fixed names: getValue and setValue.
Each gets the owning object, and the KProperty, which carries the property's name.
Here is what the compiler writes for that one line, read back as Java.
First, a hidden field, status$delegate.
It holds the delegate, the object after by.
The getter calls getValue on it.
The setter calls setValue on it.
Both calls pass this, the order, and a KProperty for status.
The compiler builds those KProperty objects once per class, in a static array called $$delegatedProperties.
Now watch it run.
Each Order holds its own Audited object, in that hidden field.
Set the status.
In the bytecode that is a call to setStatus.
setStatus calls setValue on the delegate, with the order, the KProperty and the new value.
The delegate takes the name from the KProperty, prints the change, and keeps the new value.
Read it back, and getStatus calls getValue.
The value comes back as T, so the getter casts it to String.
That hidden field is the price.
A delegate like Audited is one extra object per property, in every instance.
Three orders, three Audited objects.
The KProperty array is made once, for the whole class.
Java has no by.
There you write the same forwarding yourself, and pass the name as a string.
From the outside, both are a plain getter and setter.
A setter that logs or validates looks exactly like one that doesn't.
